Longer
LAWNG-er
adj./adv. (comparative of long)
Anglo-Saxon lang, extended in space or time — comparative degree, of greater duration or extent.

Biblical Definition

She could not longer hide him. They could not any longer stand before their enemies. What should I wait for the LORD any longer? The LORD could no longer bear.

No longer marks the breaking point where endurance gives way, and Scripture uses it at some of its most decisive turns. Jochebed's could not longer hide him is the hinge of the whole exodus narrative: the moment concealment fails is the moment Moses is set adrift, and providence, not the mother's ingenuity, carries him from there. Israel's could not any longer stand before their enemies names covenant unfaithfulness reaching its consequence under the judges. The unnamed king's any longer in 2 Kings voices the despair of a starving, besieged Samaria giving up on the LORD's deliverance almost at the moment it arrives. And Jeremiah's could no longer bear is spoken of God Himself, patience exhausted by persistent, unrepented sin, immediately followed by the desolation Judah has stored up.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from LONG: of great extent in space or duration; comparative degree, of greater duration.

expand to see more

LONG, a. Extended in space, or in time; not short.

Continued or protracted; as, a long debate.

LONGER, a. Comparative of Long; of greater duration or extent.

No longer: a phrase marking the cessation of a preceding state or the exhaustion of endurance.

Applied in Scripture to human concealment failing (Exodus), covenant strength failing (Judges), human patience failing (2 Kings), and divine patience reaching its limit (Jeremiah).

Key Scripture

Exo 2:3 — "And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink."

Jdg 2:14 — "And the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them, and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about, so that they could not any longer stand before their enemies."

2Ki 6:33 — "And while he yet talked with them, behold, the messenger came down unto him: and he said, Behold, this evil is of the LORD; what should I wait for the LORD any longer?"

Jer 44:22 — "So that the LORD could no longer bear, because of the evil of your doings, and because of the abominations which ye have committed; therefore is your land a desolation, and an astonishment, and a curse, without an inhabitant, as at this day."

Modern Corruption

A therapeutic reading of divine patience treats God's could no longer bear as an anthropomorphic embarrassment to be explained away, when Jeremiah presents it as the sober conclusion of real, righteous judgment.

expand to see more

Modern discomfort with divine wrath sometimes recasts the LORD could no longer bear as primitive or merely figurative, distancing the text from a God who actually judges sin. Jeremiah offers the phrase as the hinge of an entire historical argument: the desolation of the land is because of, not despite, the LORD's righteous exhaustion of patience with persistent evil.

The corrective is to hold divine patience and divine justice together as Scripture does: the LORD is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish, yet His patience has a real limit reached by real, unrepented sin, and that limit is itself an act of justice, not a loss of temper.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Jeremiah's could no longer bear renders lo yakol se'th (Heb.), was not able to bear or carry, the same verb used of a burden too heavy to lift.

expand to see more

Longer in Exodus marks the failure of human concealment at the hinge of the exodus story.

Longer in Judges marks covenant unfaithfulness reaching its military consequence.

Longer in 2 Kings voices human despair on the very edge of deliverance.

Longer in Jeremiah is spoken of God's own patience reaching its righteous limit.

The Hebrew behind Jeremiah's phrase pictures a burden no longer able to be carried.

Usage

"She could not longer hide him — the hinge moment of the exodus narrative."

"They could not any longer stand before their enemies — covenant unfaithfulness under the judges."

"The LORD could no longer bear — divine patience reaching its righteous limit in Jeremiah."
